newsitem.title: TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO: Trinidad, Venezuela border dispute simmering.
newsitem.headline: Trinidad, Venezuela border dispute simmering.

text.p: A border dispute between the Caribbean state of Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela has flared again with the islands' government accusing Venezuelan security forces of provocations.

After two incidents last week in the Gulf of Paria involving the Venezuelan National Guard, Foreign Minister Ralph Maraj said Trinidad and Tobago would take the dispute to the Organisation of American States.

The gulf separates Venezuela and Trinidad and Tobago by about seven miles (11 km) at their closest point. Its waters teem with fish and shrimp and both countries have oil rigs there. It has been a scene of periodic conflicts involving fishermen from both sides.

In the first incident last week, Maraj said Venezuelan guardsmen opened fire on a Trinidadian fishing boat, and in the other they seized five Trinidadian vessels and took the fishermen to the eastern Venezuelan river town of Pedernales.
Trinidad's Coast Guard said the boats were in their own territorial waters at the time.

The incidents came two weeks after Prime Minister Basdeo Panday went to Caracas for talks with Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera following a raid on a Trinidadian oil rig and the arrest of local fishermen and their boats.

Panday said he and Caldera agreed that violence was not the way to resolve the dispute and that tension had eased as a result of the meeting, but he described the oil rig search as a violation of Trinidad's sovereignty. Venezuela made no immediate statement on the latest incidents.

A new fishing treaty was negotiated this month to replace one that expired in December. It would allow fishermen from both countries to fish in each other's waters but it has yet to be ratified by either parliament.

Caracas has said no Trinidadian or Venezuelan boats will be permitted to operate in areas where oil drilling operations were to begin. That stance has upset Trinidadian fishermen and left open the possibilty of further confrontations.
Both countries are members of the 3-year-old Association of Caribbean States.
